q: The SI unit of work is the joule. One joule is equal to:
x: Work = force × displacement, so 1 J = 1 N × 1 m = 1 N m. The newton-second is the unit of impulse, and kg m s⁻¹ is the unit of momentum.

q: A force of 20 N acts on a body at 60° to its displacement of 5 m. The work done by the force is (cos 60° = 0.5):
x: W = Fd cos θ = 20 × 5 × 0.5 = 50 J. Using sin 60° instead of cos 60° gives the wrong value 50√3 J.

q: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed. The work done by the tension (centripetal force) in one revolution is:
o: Equal to the kinetic energy of the stone
Negative and equal to the kinetic energy
x: The centripetal force always acts towards the centre, at 90° to the displacement at every instant, and cos 90° = 0, so it does no work.

q: A man carries a 10 kg bag on his head and walks 20 m along a level road at constant velocity. The work done by the upward force he exerts on the bag is:
x: The upward force is perpendicular to the horizontal displacement (θ = 90°), so W = Fd cos 90° = 0, even though he may feel tired.

q: Work is a scalar quantity because it is:
o: The vector (cross) product of force and displacement
The scalar (dot) product of force and displacement
The product of force and time
The ratio of force to displacement
x: W = F · d = Fd cos θ. The dot product of two vectors gives a scalar; the cross product would give a vector.

q: A 5 kg mass is lifted vertically upward through 2 m at constant speed. The work done by the lifting force is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: At constant speed the lifting force equals the weight, mg = 5 × 10 = 50 N. W = 50 × 2 = 100 J. Forgetting g gives 10 J.

q: The force on a body increases uniformly from 0 to 40 N while the body moves 5 m in the direction of the force. The work done is:
x: Work is the area under the force–displacement graph, here a triangle: ½ × 40 × 5 = 100 J. Using the maximum force for the whole distance gives 200 J.

q: A box slides along a rough floor. The work done on the box by the force of friction is:
o: Positive, because friction acts along the displacement
Zero, because friction is perpendicular to the displacement
Negative, because friction acts opposite to the displacement
Zero, because the box keeps moving
x: Friction acts opposite to the motion, so θ = 180° and cos 180° = −1; the work done by friction is negative.

q: The dimensions of work are:
x: Work = force × distance = [MLT⁻²][L] = [ML²T⁻²]. [MLT⁻²] is force and [ML²T⁻³] is power.

q: A constant force of 30 N moves a body through 4 m and does 60 J of work. The angle between the force and the displacement is:
x: cos θ = W/(Fd) = 60/(30 × 4) = 0.5, so θ = 60°. At 0° the work would be 120 J.

q: Energy of a body is defined as its:
x: A body has energy if it is able to do work. The rate of doing work is power.

q: One kilowatt-hour (kWh) is equal to:
x: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. Forgetting to change hours into seconds or kilowatts into watts gives the smaller values.

q: Which of the following is NOT a unit of energy?
x: The watt (J s⁻¹) is a unit of power. The joule, kilowatt-hour and electron volt all measure energy.

q: The law of conservation of energy states that:
o: Energy is always converted completely into useful work
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed from one form to another
The kinetic energy of a system always remains constant
Energy can be created when work is done on a body
x: In an isolated system the total energy stays constant; energy only changes form. Kinetic energy alone need not stay constant.

q: A ball falls freely from a height with no air resistance. As it falls:
o: Its potential energy decreases, its kinetic energy increases, and the total stays constant
Its potential and kinetic energies both decrease
Its potential energy increases and its kinetic energy decreases
x: Without air resistance, the loss of gravitational potential energy equals the gain of kinetic energy, so the total mechanical energy is constant.

q: In a hydroelectric power station, the energy changes in the correct order are:
o: Kinetic energy of water → potential energy of water → electrical energy
Potential energy of stored water → kinetic energy of water → electrical energy
Chemical energy → heat energy → electrical energy
Electrical energy → kinetic energy → potential energy
x: Water stored at a height has gravitational potential energy; it falls and gains kinetic energy, which turns the turbines and the generator to give electrical energy.

q: A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance, its kinetic energy when it is 5 m above the ground is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: KE gained = loss in PE = mg(20 − 5) = 2 × 10 × 15 = 300 J. Using h = 5 m gives 100 J, and the total energy is 400 J.

q: A body at rest on a smooth (frictionless) horizontal surface has 50 J of work done on it by a horizontal force. The body:
o: Gains no energy, because the surface is horizontal
x: With no friction and no change in height, all the work done on the body appears as kinetic energy (work–energy principle).

q: Which statement about energy is correct?
o: It is a scalar quantity with the same unit as work
It is a vector quantity with the same unit as work
It is a scalar quantity with the same unit as power
It is a vector quantity with the same unit as momentum
x: Energy has magnitude only, so it is a scalar, and it is measured in joules like work, since energy is the capacity to do work.

q: The kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with speed v is:
x: KE = ½mv², the energy a body has because of its motion. The quantity mv is momentum, not energy.

q: A 2 kg trolley moves at 3 m s⁻¹. Its kinetic energy is:
x: KE = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 18 J; forgetting to square v gives 3 J.

q: If the speed of a car is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes:
x: KE ∝ v², so doubling v multiplies KE by 2² = 4.

q: The kinetic energy of a body of mass m in terms of its momentum p is:
x: KE = ½mv² and p = mv, so v = p/m and KE = ½m(p/m)² = p²/2m.

q: Two bodies of masses m and 4m have equal kinetic energies. The ratio of the momentum of the lighter body to that of the heavier body is:
x: p = √(2m × KE), so p ∝ √m when KE is equal: √m : √(4m) = 1 : 2.

q: A 1000 kg car speeds up from 10 m s⁻¹ to 20 m s⁻¹. The net work done on the car is:
x: By the work–energy theorem, W = ΔKE = ½ × 1000 × (20² − 10²) = 500 × 300 = 1.5 × 10⁵ J. Using (Δv)² = 10² gives 5 × 10⁴ J.

q: Kinetic energy can never be negative because:
o: It is measured from a reference level
Mass is positive and v² cannot be negative
x: KE = ½mv²; mass is positive and the square of any velocity is positive or zero. Velocity itself can be negative, but v² cannot.

q: A bullet of mass 0.02 kg moves at 100 m s⁻¹. Its kinetic energy is:
x: KE = ½ × 0.02 × 100² = 0.01 × 10⁴ = 100 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 200 J.

q: If the kinetic energy of a body increases by 300%, its momentum increases by:
x: An increase of 300% makes KE four times. Since p ∝ √KE for fixed mass, p becomes 2 times, an increase of 100%.

q: A ball is thrown vertically upward. At its highest point its kinetic energy is:
o: Maximum, and its potential energy is zero
Zero, and all its energy is potential
Equal to its initial kinetic energy
x: At the top of a vertical throw the ball is momentarily at rest, so v = 0 and KE = 0; its initial KE has become gravitational PE.

q: Potential energy is the energy possessed by a body because of its:
x: Potential energy is stored energy due to position (as in a gravitational field) or configuration (as in a compressed spring). Energy due to motion is kinetic energy.

q: Which of the following is an example of potential energy that is NOT gravitational potential energy?
o: Energy of water held behind a dam
Energy of a book on a high shelf
Energy stored in a compressed spring
Energy of a stone raised above the ground
x: A compressed spring stores elastic potential energy due to its configuration. The other three have energy due to their height in Earth's gravitational field.

q: A 3 kg box is raised 4 m vertically. The gain in its gravitational potential energy is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: ΔU = mgh = 3 × 10 × 4 = 120 J. Leaving out g gives 12 J.

q: Gravitational potential energy is the potential energy a body has because of:
o: Its speed in a gravitational field
Its position in a gravitational field
The stretching or compressing of the body
x: Gravitational PE depends on where a mass is in a gravitational field. Stretching or compressing gives elastic PE, and charge gives electric PE.

q: A body is taken from point X to a higher point Y, once along a straight path and once along a winding path. The work done against gravity is:
x: Gravity is a conservative force: the work done against it depends only on the starting and finishing heights, not on the path taken.

q: A body is moved around a closed path in Earth's gravitational field and returns to its starting point. The total work done by gravity is:
o: Equal to mgh for the highest point
Equal to the weight times the path length
x: Gravity is conservative, so the work done by it around any closed path is zero; the body returns to the same height with the same gravitational PE.

q: The formula ΔU = mgh for the change in gravitational potential energy is valid only when:
o: The height is small compared with the radius of the Earth
The body is moving at constant speed
The body is above the surface of the Moon
The mass of the body is small
x: mgh assumes g is constant. This is true only for heights much smaller than Earth's radius; for large distances the absolute PE −GMm/r must be used.

q: Which statement is correct?
o: Potential energy always means gravitational potential energy
Gravitational potential energy depends on the speed of the body
Elastic potential energy is a kind of gravitational potential energy
Gravitational potential energy is one kind of potential energy
x: Potential energy is the general term for stored energy of position or configuration; gravitational, elastic and electric PE are its kinds.

q: A charged particle held near another fixed charge has:
x: The energy stored because of the position of a charge in an electric field is electric potential energy, another kind of PE that is not gravitational.

q: A 2 kg block slides 10 m down a smooth incline that makes 30° with the horizontal. Its loss of gravitational potential energy is (g = 10 m s⁻², sin 30° = 0.5):
x: Vertical drop h = 10 sin 30° = 5 m, so ΔU = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J. Using the length along the slope gives 200 J; using cos 30° gives 100√3 J.

q: The gravitational potential energy of a body placed exactly at the chosen reference level is:
x: The reference level is, by definition, the level where gravitational PE is taken as zero.

q: A 2 kg ball lies 3 m below a table top that is chosen as the reference level. Its gravitational potential energy is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: U = mgh with h = −3 m: 2 × 10 × (−3) = −60 J. Below the reference level, gravitational PE is negative.

q: The gravitational potential energy of a body is negative when the body is:
o: At rest on the reference level
x: PE is measured from the reference level: positive above it, zero on it and negative below it. The direction of motion does not decide the sign.

q: Changing the reference level from the floor to the ceiling of a room changes:
o: The value of the potential energy of a body, but not the change in its potential energy between two points
The change in potential energy between two points, but not its value at a point
Both the value and the change in potential energy
Neither the value nor the change in potential energy
x: The value of PE at a point depends on where zero is chosen, but the difference in PE between two points depends only on their height difference.

q: For absolute gravitational potential energy, the zero of potential energy is taken at:
x: Absolute PE is measured from a point infinitely far from the Earth, where the gravitational force and the PE are both zero.

q: The absolute gravitational potential energy of a body near the Earth is negative because:
o: The body is always moving towards the Earth
The mass of the body is taken as negative
Gravitational potential energy is a vector pointing downward
The force is attractive, so work must be done on the body to take it to infinity where PE is zero
x: Since gravity attracts, energy must be supplied to move the body out to infinity, where U = 0. So at any finite distance its PE is less than zero.

q: A 1 kg book is on a shelf 2 m above the floor. A table top 0.8 m above the floor is taken as the reference level. The potential energy of the book is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Height above the reference level = 2 − 0.8 = 1.2 m, so U = 1 × 10 × 1.2 = 12 J. Measuring from the floor would give 20 J.

q: A 1 kg body is raised from 5 m below the reference level to 5 m above it. The change in its potential energy is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: U changes from 1 × 10 × (−5) = −50 J to +50 J, so ΔU = +50 − (−50) = +100 J. Adding the two values gives the wrong answer zero.

q: As a satellite moves farther from the Earth, its absolute gravitational potential energy:
o: Increases, becoming less negative and approaching zero
Increases and becomes large and positive
x: U = −GMm/r. As r increases, U gets closer to zero from below, so it increases, but it never becomes positive.

q: The absolute gravitational potential energy of a mass m on the surface of the Earth (mass M, radius R) is:
x: Absolute PE = −GMm/r with r = R at the surface. −GMm/R² is the form of the force, and −GM/R has no mass of the body, so it is not an energy.

q: Power is defined as:
o: The product of force and time
The work done per unit displacement
x: P = W/t, the work done per unit time. The ability to do work is energy, and work per unit displacement is force.

q: One horsepower is approximately equal to:
x: 1 hp ≈ 746 W. It is a unit of power, so it cannot be given in joules.

q: A force of 200 N keeps a cart moving at 5 m s⁻¹ in the direction of the force. The power delivered is:
x: P = F · v = Fv cos 0° = 200 × 5 = 1000 W. Dividing F by v gives 40, which is not power.

q: A force of 100 N acts on a body at 60° to its velocity of 4 m s⁻¹. The power delivered is (cos 60° = 0.5):
x: P = Fv cos θ = 100 × 4 × 0.5 = 200 W. Ignoring the angle gives 400 W; using sin 60° gives 200√3 W.

q: Power is a scalar quantity because it is:
o: The scalar product of force and velocity
The vector product of force and velocity
The product of force and time
The ratio of velocity to force
x: P = F · v = Fv cos θ. The dot product of two vectors is a scalar.

q: A motor lifts a 50 kg load vertically through 10 m in 10 s at constant speed. The power of the motor is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Work = mgh = 50 × 10 × 10 = 5000 J; P = 5000/10 = 500 W. Forgetting to divide by time gives 5000.

q: A car engine delivers 30 kW while the car moves at a constant 20 m s⁻¹ on a level road. The total resistive force on the car is:
x: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistance. P = Fv, so F = P/v = 30 000/20 = 1500 N. Forgetting that 30 kW = 30 000 W gives 1.5 N.

q: The dimensions of power are:
x: P = work/time = [ML²T⁻²]/[T] = [ML²T⁻³]. [ML²T⁻²] is work or energy.

q: Crane X lifts a load to a certain height in 10 s; crane Y lifts the same load to the same height in 20 s. The power of crane X compared with crane Y is:
x: Both do the same work, but P = W/t, so the crane taking half the time has twice the power.

q: A 2 kg body starts from rest on a smooth surface and is pushed by a constant 4 N force. The power delivered by the force at t = 3 s is:
x: a = F/m = 2 m s⁻², so v = at = 6 m s⁻¹ at 3 s, and P = Fv = 4 × 6 = 24 W. 12 W is the average power over the 3 s.

q: When a body is pushed along a rough floor, the work done against friction is mainly converted into:
x: Work done against friction is dissipated as heat (internal energy) in the body, the floor and the surroundings.

q: A box is pushed 4 m at constant speed across a rough floor against a friction force of 10 N. The heat produced is:
x: Heat produced = work done against friction = f × d = 10 × 4 = 40 J. At constant speed the KE does not change.

q: A block sliding on a rough horizontal surface slows down and stops. Its initial kinetic energy is:
o: Converted into heat by the work done against friction
Stored as elastic energy in the block
x: Energy is not destroyed: friction does negative work on the block, and its kinetic energy is changed into heat in the block, the surface and the surroundings.

q: A 2 kg block slides at 6 m s⁻¹ on a rough level floor and stops after 9 m. The average friction force on it is:
x: Work against friction = initial KE: f × 9 = ½ × 2 × 6² = 36 J, so f = 4 N. Forgetting the ½ in KE gives 8 N.

q: A body slides down a rough inclined plane. Which energy statement is correct?
o: Loss of potential energy = gain of kinetic energy
Gain of kinetic energy = loss of potential energy + work done against friction
Loss of potential energy = work done against friction only, whatever the speed
Loss of potential energy = gain of kinetic energy + work done against friction
x: Part of the lost gravitational PE becomes KE and part is used against friction and dissipated as heat, so the KE gained is less than the PE lost.

q: A 1 kg stone falls from a height of 20 m and reaches the ground at 18 m s⁻¹. The energy dissipated against air resistance is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: PE lost = 1 × 10 × 20 = 200 J; KE gained = ½ × 1 × 18² = 162 J. Energy lost to air resistance = 200 − 162 = 38 J.

q: Rubbing the palms together quickly makes them warm because:
o: Work done against friction is converted into heat
Heat flows from the air into the hands
The kinetic energy of the hands becomes potential energy
x: The work done against friction between the palms is dissipated as heat. Energy is converted, not created.

q: Most meteors burn up high in the atmosphere. This is because:
o: Air contains enough oxygen to make rocks burn at any speed
Work done against air resistance at very high speed produces a large amount of heat
Gravitational potential energy changes directly into light
The meteors lose mass by evaporation in sunlight
x: A meteor moves through the air at very high speed; the work done against air resistance (a resistive medium) is dissipated as heat, which makes it glow and burn.

q: A crate is dragged at constant speed along a floor with constant friction. If it is dragged twice the distance, the heat produced by friction becomes:
x: Heat produced = friction force × distance. With the same friction force, doubling the distance doubles the heat.

q: Which statement about energy dissipated as heat by friction is correct?
o: It is destroyed, so total energy decreases
It is stored as potential energy in the surface
It can always be fully changed back into kinetic energy
It spreads into the surroundings and cannot be fully recovered as useful work, though total energy is conserved
x: The total energy stays constant, but heat spread into the environment is no longer available as useful energy.

q: The efficiency of a machine is defined as:
o: Useful output energy ÷ total input energy × 100%
Total input energy ÷ useful output energy × 100%
Useful output energy − total input energy
x: Efficiency = (useful output / total input) × 100%. It is a ratio, not a difference.

q: An electric motor takes in 500 J of electrical energy and gives out 400 J of useful mechanical work. Its efficiency is:
x: Efficiency = 400/500 × 100% = 80%. 125% comes from turning the ratio upside down, and 20% is the fraction wasted.

q: The efficiency of a practical machine is always less than 100% because:
o: Energy is destroyed inside the machine
The output energy is always greater than the input
Some input energy is lost, mostly as heat due to friction
x: In real devices some energy is always dissipated, mainly as heat through friction, so useful output is less than input. Energy is not destroyed.

q: A machine of efficiency 60% is given 200 J of energy. The energy wasted is:
x: Useful output = 0.60 × 200 = 120 J, so the energy wasted = 200 − 120 = 80 J. 120 J is the useful output, not the waste.

q: An electric pump of input power 1000 W lifts 100 kg of water through 6 m in 10 s. The efficiency of the pump is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Useful power = mgh/t = 100 × 10 × 6/10 = 600 W; efficiency = 600/1000 × 100% = 60%. 40% is the fraction wasted.

q: Efficiency has:
o: No unit, because it is a ratio of two energies
x: Efficiency is output energy divided by input energy (or output power by input power), so the units cancel; it is a pure number or percentage.

q: A filament lamp becomes hot when it is lit. This shows that:
o: All the electrical energy is changed into light
Energy is being created in the filament
The lamp has an efficiency greater than 100%
Part of the electrical energy is changed into heat, so its efficiency as a light source is less than 100%
x: Only part of the input energy becomes useful light; the rest is dissipated as heat, so the lamp's efficiency is well below 100%.

q: A motor of efficiency 80% must supply a useful output power of 400 W. Its input power must be:
x: Input = output/efficiency = 400/0.8 = 500 W. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 320 W.

q: Oiling the moving parts of a machine increases its efficiency because:
o: It reduces friction, so less input energy is wasted as heat
It adds energy from the oil to the output
It changes heat back into useful work
x: Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts, so less energy is dissipated as heat and a larger fraction of the input becomes useful output.
